reports.title: Thankfulness: so much to be thankful for
reports.text:
Cooler temperatures are just one reason to be thankful
N ovember is a month I’m thankful to see roll around every year. The cooler temperatures and frosty mornings are a reprieve from the intense heat domes we’ve suffered through these past summers. July and August triple-digit readings have forced me to sweat profusely instead of lightly perspiring. It’s wonderful to stand in cold water, chilled, and try to catch a trout on a fly. Exhaling slowly, I watch my damp breath turn into ice crystals and disappear. What a beautiful morning to be here. Quiet, alone, and time to ponder the things I’ve been too busy to think about otherwise.

reports.title: Kentucky Throws “Christmas for the Fishes,” Increases Habitat And Fish Populations
reports.text:
For most people, Christmas trees have a relatively short lifespan once they’re harvested for sale. They spend a few weeks brightening up living rooms before being unceremoniously dragged to the curb or taken to a recycling center. But in Kentucky, those post-holiday evergreens have an entirely different destination: the bottom of a lake.
Through an initiative called “ Christmas for the Fishes ,” the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR) collects thousands of Christmas trees each year and sinks them into reservoirs throughout the state. What might otherwise become yard waste gets a second life as valuable fish habitat.

reports.title: The Three Best Crawfish Imitators to Use for Catching Bass This Winter
reports.text:
There are all kinds of reasons why winter is a great time to target bass with crawfish-imitating baits.
For starters, bass like to hang along the rocky bottoms in five to 30 feet, where crawfish are often plentiful in colder months. And as water temps approach 40 degrees, the crawfish become dormant — making them easy meals to pick off. This means that bass, which are also trying to conserve energy, don’t have to strain for a high-protein crawfish meal.
With all of that in mind, let’s look at some of the best craw imitators to fish with this winter.

reports.text:

reports.title: GALLERY: Morrison hoists the winning bass at the Toyota Series Championship
reports.text:
COUNCE, Tenn. – Weighing in last but coming in first, Tallis Morrison dropped 19 pounds, 10 ounces on Championship Day to win the Toyota Series Championship on Pickwick Lake. Morrison’s three-day total of 58-15 was just enough to put him over Hayden O’Barr’s 58-6. Check out the scene as the Georgia angler hoisted the trophy and celebrated a $200,000 payday and an invitation to REDCREST 2027.
This event is presented by Phoenix Boats and hosted by Explore Pickwick Lake – Hardin County Tourism and Bill Dance Signature Lakes.

reports.title: CN How To Nov 2026 How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
reports.text:
How To: Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie behavior.
In this episode of The Playbook, Crappie Dan explains how shadows, current, and underwater structure influence crappie and bass behavior. Fish often face into the current, positioning themselves where baitfish will naturally approach. During sunny conditions, they tend to hold in the shade created by stumps, brush, overhanging trees, and shoreline drop-offs, often near the edge of the light.
The key to success is proper boat positioning and bait placement. When casting or jigging, position your bait up current so it moves naturally toward the fish. Approaching from behind can spook them…

reports.title: Hit Lake Murray’s brush for fall crappie
reports.text:
Don’t miss the fall crappie bite
A s Lake Murray’s water temperature cools down in October, Capt. Brad Taylor of Taylor Outdoors said the crappie fishing gets cranked up.
“October is a great month because you can catch crappie in a number of ways, really just about any way you want to catch them will work,” he said.
One way Taylor targets them this time of year is by fishing brush in the main river channel.
“Fall is kind of a magical time of year for Lake Murray because the shad start working up the river,” he said. “And the crappie follow the bait. If you can find the bait, which isn’t too difficult using electronics, then you can find the crappie.”

Matching your jig to the size and shape of the main crappie forage can greatly increase your number of hookups.
Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
By Keith Sutton
One of the simplest ways to improve your crappie fishing is to give the fish what they’re already looking for. That means matching your jig to the size and general shape of the forage crappie are feeding on.
If 2-inch minnows make up a big part of the crappie diet in the lake you’re fishing, for example, a 2-inch jig is a logical choice. If the fish are eating tiny shiners, you’ll probably do better with a smaller offering. The same principle applies when shad, fathead minnows or other forage dominate the menu.
